title: Christmas Wishes

jokes.text: Andy introduces himself as 'the first office Santa ever to make holiday wishes come true' while clearly wearing a Santa suit and taking his role extremely seriously
jokes.setup: Andy announces himself with grandiose pride as if this is a historic achievement
jokes.punchline: The self-importance of calling himself the 'first ever' to do this mundane office thing undercuts the triviality of the role
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy self-aggrandizement played straight. Works because it's character-specific but isn't a particularly sharp joke.

jokes.text: Stanley's talking head: 'I've been here 18 years and I've suffered through some weird, thematic Christmases. A Honolulu Christmas, a Pulp Fiction Christmas, a Muslim Christmas, Moroccan Christmas, Mo Rocca Christmas.'
jokes.setup: Stanley catalogues the absurd themed Christmases he's been forced to endure over 18 years
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from merely odd to 'Mo Rocca Christmas' — a TV pundit shoehorned in as a holiday theme — which is the absurdist non-sequitur payoff
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional list comedy. The escalation from 'Honolulu Christmas' to 'Pulp Fiction Christmas' to 'Muslim Christmas' to 'Moroccan Christmas' to 'Mo Rocca Christmas' is a perfectly constructed joke: each entry is funnier than the last, and the final beat exploits the near-homophone between 'Moroccan' and 'Mo Rocca' (the CBS Sunday Morning correspondent) for a surreal, absurdist payoff. It's deeply character-specific — only Stanley's long-suffering, deadpan perspective makes this land. The economy is tight and the originality is high. This is the episode's best written joke.

jokes.text: Stanley: 'I got Stanley tickets to see Lewis Black for his birthday. Might not have been the best idea.'
jokes.setup: Andy tries to justify understanding Stanley's worldview by saying he got him Lewis Black tickets
jokes.punchline: The deadpan admission that an angry, shouting comedian was perhaps not the best gift for Stanley — implied by Stanley's continued rage — is the understated payoff
jokes.explanation: Nice beat — Andy's self-undermining confession works because it implies he thought Lewis Black would CALM Stanley down, which reveals how oblivious Andy is. Solid character joke, not exceptional.

jokes.text: Stanley: 'I don't want no Kwanzaa wreath. I don't need a dreidel in my face. And who's that black Santa for? I don't care. I know Santa ain't black. I could care less.'
jokes.setup: Stanley is ranting about unwanted inclusive holiday decorations
jokes.punchline: Stanley, a Black man, dismisses 'black Santa' and 'Kwanzaa' with complete indifference — the joke is that he wants nothing but traditional (white) Christmas imagery, subverting the expected position
jokes.explanation: Good subversive character comedy. Stanley's rejection of well-intentioned multicultural gestures is a running character note and works because it's specific to his curmudgeonly persona. The 'I could care less' (a malapropism for 'couldn't care less') may be intentional character voice.

jokes.text: Stanley: 'I want Christmas. Just give me plain baby Jesus lying in a manger Christmas.'
jokes.setup: Stanley has been ranting about all the unwanted holiday alternatives
jokes.punchline: His impassioned plea for 'plain baby Jesus' Christmas as the finale of the rant — delivered with total sincerity and exhaustion — is the button on the whole confessional
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Stanley confessional sequence. Works as the payoff to the escalating list, but slightly less surprising than the Mo Rocca moment.

jokes.text: Andy reveals he brought his bicycle to be Erin's designated driver 'in the event that you drink too much, which is by no means required'
jokes.setup: Andy is granting holiday wishes as Santa; Erin's apparent wish was a designated driver
jokes.punchline: The designated driver is a bicycle — completely impractical — delivered with Andy's characteristic sincerity and the qualifier that drinking 'is by no means required'
jokes.explanation: Absurdist touch that works — a bicycle as a designated driver solution is charmingly idiotic, very Andy. The disclaimer softens it in a funny way.

jokes.text: An unnamed character's Christmas wish is to not attend 'meetings that degrade our sense of adulthood' — Andy says he can't grant it but did get them an acre of property on the moon
jokes.setup: Andy cannot fulfill the wish about meetings, so he pivots to an alternative gift
jokes.punchline: The moon property is the absurd consolation prize, and the employee then asks specific real-estate questions (dark side or light side? by the Sea of Tranquility?) treating it completely seriously
jokes.explanation: The escalating specificity of the moon real estate questions is the best part — 'Is it by the Sea of Tranquility? Directly adjacent. Beachfront.' is a tight absurdist exchange that commits to the bit.

jokes.text: Andy's biggest wish is that everyone get along with his girlfriend Jessica, then: 'She's not your grandmother, is she?' / 'Ugh, gam gam's name is Ruth, Jim. You should know. I introduced you on speaker phone that time.'
jokes.setup: Andy emotionally declares his biggest wish is for people to like Jessica
jokes.punchline: Jim's needling question about whether Jessica is Andy's grandmother, and Andy's flustered, specific rebuttal with 'gam gam's name is Ruth' — the detail that he introduced Jim to her 'on speaker phone that time' is peak Andy obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Jim's trolling of Andy is classic dynamic, but what elevates it is Andy's specific, hurt rebuttal — 'gam gam's name is Ruth' spoken with genuine offense, and 'I introduced you on speaker phone that time' implying an absurd level of intimacy for a phone introduction. Character-rich.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Jessica is my super serious girlfriend who is seriously awesome and seriously sexy. Only thing that's not serious, by the way, our repartee.'
jokes.setup: Andy is overselling Jessica to the group
jokes.punchline: The earnest use of 'repartee' to describe his relationship banter, implying he thinks of himself as witty and playful, is self-undermining given how uncool Andy is
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny character beat — Andy trying to seem sophisticated and cool falls flat in an endearing way.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Hey, what's Ruth's deal, man? Totally out of your league.'
jokes.setup: Andy just got flustered about his grandmother Ruth being confused with his girlfriend
jokes.punchline: Jim pivots to pretending to be interested in the grandmother as a romantic prospect, calling her 'out of Andy's league'
jokes.explanation: Quick and punchy callback. Jim's economy with the punchline is sharp — 'totally out of your league' applied to the grandmother is a good button.

jokes.text: Andy: 'mistletoe is not an excuse for sexual assault. And don't go near gam gam.'
jokes.setup: Andy is wrapping up his Santa address with holiday rules
jokes.punchline: The sudden pivot from cheerful holiday advice to 'mistletoe is not an excuse for sexual assault' is jarring and funny; followed immediately by 'don't go near gam gam' — continuing the grandmother joke
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one line. The sexual assault disclaimer is a good dark subversive beat — it implies this has been a real problem at past office parties. The 'don't go near gam gam' callback to Jim's flirtatious interest in Ruth is a solid button.

jokes.text: Erin talking head: 'I love Jessica, and I haven't even met her yet. It's like, we don't even need to meet, you know? I already love you. Stay home.'
jokes.setup: Erin presents herself as enthusiastically welcoming Andy's girlfriend
jokes.punchline: 'Stay home' — the sudden pivot from professed love to wanting her to not come at all, delivered with Erin's characteristic naive directness
jokes.explanation: This is excellent character comedy. Erin's emotional logic is perfectly constructed: the buildup of 'I love Jessica, we don't even need to meet, I already love you' sets up a warmth that makes 'Stay home' land like a gut punch. It's simultaneously sweet, jealous, and completely unself-aware — pure Erin. High economy, well-structured, deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Kelly: 'Just want you to know that I will be mean to Jessica, if you want me to be. Oh, no, no, it's fine, Kelly. It's really no problem. I was already planning on being mean to her.'
jokes.setup: Kelly offers to be mean to Jessica as a favor to Erin
jokes.punchline: Before anyone can respond, Kelly clarifies that she's already planning to be mean to Jessica regardless — the 'offer' was performative
jokes.explanation: The joke structure is Kelly playing both sides of the dialogue — offering, then pre-rejecting her own offer, then admitting the offer was cover for her existing intention. Funny and character-specific to Kelly's scheming-but-transparent personality.

jokes.text: Kelly wishes Erin 'Happy Pancha Ganapati' — Erin asks 'Ew, what is that?' — Kelly explains it's a five-day Hindu celebration honoring Ganesh, patron of the arts — Erin: 'Cool.'
jokes.setup: Kelly greets Erin with a real but obscure Hindu holiday
jokes.punchline: Erin's 'Ew, what is that?' followed by complete acceptance of the explanation ('Cool') — the 'ew' implies disgust but she has no follow-through objection
jokes.explanation: Minor character beat. Erin's 'ew' is slightly funny as an unconscious reaction, and the quick pivot to 'Cool' is a small character moment. Not a strong joke but qualifies as a comedic beat.

jokes.text: Robert California, consoled about his wife leaving: 'I actually appreciate the human intimacy. I feel like a kitten being cradled by a gorilla.'
jokes.setup: Kevin bluntly brings up Robert's wife leaving him
jokes.punchline: Robert's poetic, self-aware response comparing himself to a kitten being held by a gorilla — an image that is both vulnerable and slightly terrifying — is perfectly Robert California
jokes.explanation: This is genuinely exceptional character writing. The gorilla/kitten metaphor is original, evocative, and completely specific to Robert California's character — his tendency to deliver strange, literary pronouncements with total sincerity. The image works on multiple levels: it's tender (kitten = vulnerable), slightly disturbing (gorilla = clumsy, potentially crushing), and positions Robert as someone who aestheticizes his own emotional experience. Highly quotable, high rewatch value. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor example.

jokes.text: Robert California: 'It's been ten days since I had sexual intercourse.'
jokes.setup: Robert is receiving comfort from coworkers about his separation
jokes.punchline: He volunteers the precise number of days since he's had sex — wildly inappropriate oversharing delivered with his characteristic matter-of-fact gravity
jokes.explanation: The precision ('ten days') is what makes this work rather than just being a cringe overshare. Robert treating this clinical data point as relevant and worth volunteering is deeply in character. Kevin's response ('Well, you came to the right place') is unintentionally creepy and adds to the discomfort.

jokes.text: Robert California on the corporate party: 'I am so tired of the Black-Eyed Peas. It's rock and roll for people who don't like rock and roll. It's rap for people who don't like rap. It's pop for people who don't like pop.'
jokes.setup: Robert describes the wretched corporate party
jokes.punchline: His three-part dismissal of the Black-Eyed Peas — each iteration covering a different genre they nominally inhabit — is an elegant formulation of a widely-felt sentiment
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best crafted lines. The parallel three-part structure ('X for people who don't like X') is perfectly economical and the observation is sharp enough to feel true. Robert's voice elevates what could be a generic complaint into something quotable. The structure alone — using the same grammatical form three times with maximum brevity — is excellent craft. High quotability; this line clearly stuck in cultural memory.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I hate to have to take my Santa hat off and put on my hard ass hat' — then physically switches to a different hat labeled accordingly
jokes.setup: Andy signals a tonal shift from Santa to authority figure
jokes.punchline: He literally has a 'hard ass hat' — a physical prop that makes the metaphor literal — which is both an absurd visual and perfectly Andy in its over-preparedness
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag — the literalization of the idiom is a classic Office move. Works especially well in the single-camera format where we can see the actual hat. Andy's preparedness (having a labeled hat ready) is character-specific.

jokes.text: Dwight dismisses Andy's mediation: 'The weak always bully the strong, contrary to what you see in the media. I am always acting in self-defense. Occasionally preemptive self-defense.'
jokes.setup: Andy confronts Dwight about the desk prank war
jokes.punchline: 'Occasionally preemptive self-defense' — the qualifier that admits he sometimes strikes first while maintaining he's the victim is a perfect Dwight contradiction delivered deadpan
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dwight character comedy. 'Preemptive self-defense' is a perfect oxymoron that captures Dwight's self-serving logic — he genuinely believes attacking first counts as defense. The line is original within the show's context, tightly structured, and impossible to imagine coming from any other character. Quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight slaps Jim's hand reaching for something — 'Ow, what are you doing?' / 'Hey! Hey! Respect the hat.'
jokes.setup: Dwight and Jim are ostensibly cooperating for Andy's bonus threat
jokes.punchline: Dwight reflexively slaps Jim and justifies it as defending Andy's Santa hat's honor
jokes.explanation: Minor physical beat. Works because of Dwight's absurd loyalty to authority symbols ('respect the hat'), but isn't particularly clever.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I'm gonna speak in a language you both understand. Monet.' [beat] 'Money.'
jokes.setup: Andy attempts a dramatic pivot to threaten financial consequences
jokes.punchline: He mispronounces/mangles 'money' as 'Monet' (the impressionist painter), then has to correct himself — the deflation of his own dramatic moment is perfectly Andy
jokes.explanation: A small gem. Andy trying to be intimidating and accidentally saying 'Monet' (the French painter) instead of 'money' is a perfect Andy moment — he's trying to be tough and stylish, and his Cornell education backfires in a moment of overwrought dramatic tension. The beat pause before the correction sells it completely. Character-specific, economical, well-structured.

jokes.text: Jessica arrives; Erin rushes to hug her aggressively: 'We don't say hi. We hug.' and squeezes her — 'I-- Oof. Sorry.'
jokes.setup: Andy's new girlfriend arrives and meets his ex-girlfriend Erin for the first time
jokes.punchline: Erin's aggressive mandatory hug — announced as policy — is so forceful it causes an audible 'oof' from Jessica, expressing Erin's barely-suppressed hostility in the guise of extreme warmth
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy — Erin's 'We don't say hi. We hug.' is a perfect passive-aggressive assertion of dominance disguised as warmth. The physical comedy payoff (the oof) suggests she's squeezing harder than socially acceptable. Character-specific to Erin's unself-aware emotional sabotage.

jokes.text: Andy talking head: 'My ex is meeting my sex. Which is always scary. You know? And not just because you think they might talk about your penis. That's just part of it.'
jokes.setup: Andy reflects on Erin and Jessica meeting
jokes.punchline: 'Not just because you think they might talk about your penis. That's just part of it.' — the clarification that penis-discussion is merely one component of his anxiety, implying the deeper fear is also present, is a great Andy overshare
jokes.explanation: Sharp structure: the 'not just because' phrasing implies the penis concern is so foundational it goes without saying, but then he says it anyway. The qualifier 'That's just part of it' escalates the joke by suggesting there are even worse concerns he's not sharing. Quintessential Andy overshare in confessional format.

jokes.text: Erin claims spontaneous scoliosis and starts dramatically convulsing — 'Spontaneous... Scoliosis.' / 'This thing could take your arm off, your head off.'
jokes.setup: Erin invents a scoliosis story to compete with Jessica, then escalates it
jokes.punchline: The 'spontaneous scoliosis' attack is physically absurd — and her warning that it 'could take your arm off, your head off' while writhing is escalating absurdist physical comedy
jokes.explanation: Good escalating physical gag. 'Spontaneous scoliosis' is an inherently funny phrase, and Erin selling it with physical performance is very on-brand. The threat of decapitation via scoliosis is pure absurdist escalation.

jokes.text: Darryl explains the upstairs corporate party: 'There's a Christmas party upstairs tonight.' — Erin asks 'Isn't that just for popsicles?' / 'Popsicles?' / 'Yeah, like, upstairs people. 'Cause you got a stick up your butt.'
jokes.setup: Darryl describes the upstairs management Christmas party
jokes.punchline: Erin has invented the word 'popsicles' for upper management (people with 'a stick up their butt') — a malapropism/neologism that is completely Erin-brained
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Erin has independently coined 'popsicles' as slang for stiff upper-management types (because popsicles have sticks, and uptight people have sticks up their butts). The internal logic is both childlike and perfectly consistent, and when she explains it, the explanation is funnier than the word itself. This is deeply character-specific — only Erin could arrive at this neologism organically. High originality, high character integration, clean structure.

jokes.text: Erin's alternative theory: 'See, I thought it was because they're all so rich they could eat popsicles all the time. What?'
jokes.setup: Darryl questions Erin's popsicle logic
jokes.punchline: Erin reveals she had TWO competing theories for why they'd be called popsicles — the second (they can afford popsicles constantly) is charmingly incoherent and further establishes her unique logic
jokes.explanation: The callback to the popsicle theory with an alternate explanation that's equally incoherent is a perfect escalation. Erin having two separate and mutually exclusive theories, both committed to, is brilliant character comedy. The 'What?' at the end — seemingly asking herself why she thought that — adds one more beat.

jokes.text: Erin: 'You had me at clookies. I can't wait to find out what they are.'
jokes.setup: Darryl lists party amenities ending in 'cookies'
jokes.punchline: Erin mishears 'cookies' as 'clookies' — an invented word — and instead of correcting herself, commits to wondering what clookies are
jokes.explanation: Charming Erin character beat. 'You had me at clookies' riffs on the famous 'You had me at hello' (Jerry Maguire), and Erin's blithe acceptance of a word she clearly made up — genuinely curious about what clookies might be — is endearing and funny. High character integration, economical delivery.

jokes.text: Gabe, overhearing the conversation: 'I will look so handsome for you, Darryl.' — then a pause as everyone registers this
jokes.setup: Darryl is persuading Erin to come to the upstairs party
jokes.punchline: Gabe inserts himself, declaring he'll look handsome — apparently not invited, making this an awkward overstep that highlights his social desperation
jokes.explanation: Gabe's awkward social insertion is mildly funny — his neediness and the absurdity of volunteering to look handsome 'for' Darryl specifically is a character beat that registers more than it lands.

jokes.text: Jim talking head: 'Dwight really wants my bonus. He's trying to entrap me. Oh God, now I can't drink at this thing.' [pause] 'I get really pranky when I drink.'
jokes.setup: Jim acknowledges the bonus situation with Dwight
jokes.punchline: 'I get really pranky when I drink' — Jim's casual self-revelation that his pranking escalates with alcohol, delivered as an afterthought, is a nice character moment
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — 'pranky' is an inherently funny word and Jim's casual acknowledgment that alcohol intensifies this is an understated confession. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Meredith trying to get Erin to take a shot: 'The fifth one is for you, Erin. You can take it or leave it. To take it would be to accept that you're at a party and you're an adult woman with an adventurous spirit. To leave it would be fine, too.'
jokes.setup: Meredith is organizing shots and includes one for Erin
jokes.punchline: The seemingly balanced option ('to leave it would be fine, too') is delivered after an elaborate positive case for taking the shot — the 'fine' is clearly not fine, and the whole speech is peer pressure disguised as free choice
jokes.explanation: Good Meredith character moment — her barely-concealed pressure to drink, dressed up in the language of adult autonomy, is character-specific to her as the office's resident alcoholic. The structure (elaborate pro argument, deflated con) works well.

jokes.text: Erin takes the shot and yells 'Jiminy Christmas!' — Meredith echoes 'Jiminy Christmas, indeed' with satisfaction
jokes.setup: Erin takes the shot for the first time
jokes.punchline: Her wholesome exclamation ('Jiminy Christmas!') in response to alcohol — treating it like a Disney moment — followed by Meredith's satisfied echo
jokes.explanation: Sweet character moment — Erin's use of 'Jiminy Christmas' (a Pinocchio reference) for her first shot is perfectly Erin. Meredith's gravely satisfied repetition is a good reaction beat.

jokes.text: Dwight loudly recites Jim's replacement credit card number (and security code) into the phone while Jim is nearby
jokes.setup: We are clearly watching some kind of prank/setup between Jim and Dwight
jokes.punchline: Jim has faked a phone call to loudly broadcast a fake credit card number, baiting Dwight into identity theft — the specificity of the numbers being rattled off makes the joke land
jokes.explanation: Good structural prank setup — we know Jim is baiting Dwight (the camera knows, we know), and the specificity of the fake credit card numbers being read aloud is the comedic hook. The payoff comes in the next beat.

jokes.text: Jim talking head: 'Dwight did take the bait. He used my credit card numbers to send a $200 bouquet of flowers... to my wife. From me.'
jokes.setup: Jim reveals that Dwight fell for the credit card bait
jokes.punchline: Dwight's 'prank' was to send Jim's wife flowers from Jim — which is actually a nice thing — the prank backfired so completely it became a gift
jokes.explanation: Excellent prank comedy with a perfect twist. The multi-level joke: Jim baited Dwight into using the credit card → Dwight thought he'd cause chaos → Dwight's 'prank' was sending flowers to Jim's wife from Jim → which is just... thoughtful. The three-beat reveal ('to my wife. From me.') with the pauses is extremely well-paced. 'Boom!' sells it. This is the kind of Jim-Dwight prank where the subversion works on every level — Dwight loses, Jim wins, and the audience gets a structurally elegant joke. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Darryl arrives at the upstairs party in a full tuxedo — visible reaction from the upstairs crowd
jokes.setup: The invitation was 'nice, real nice — people get dressed up'
jokes.punchline: Darryl has taken 'dressed up' to mean formal tuxedo, wildly overdressed for what is apparently a business-casual corporate gathering
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag with strong character logic — Darryl, wanting to make a good impression at the fancy party, overdoes it. The physical comedy of arriving in a tuxedo to a business-casual party is a relatable comedic situation executed well.

jokes.text: Robert California to Darryl: 'I meant dressed up compared to normal. You usually dress like a Ghostbuster.'
jokes.setup: Darryl is overdressed in a tuxedo
jokes.punchline: Robert's cutting observation that Darryl normally dresses like a Ghostbuster — a hilariously specific comparison suggesting his warehouse aesthetic reads as costume-adjacent
jokes.explanation: Sharp line — 'you usually dress like a Ghostbuster' is highly specific and quotable. Robert's delivery makes it feel like a neutral observation rather than an insult, which adds to the comedy. The Ghostbuster comparison is original and specific enough to feel earned.

jokes.text: Robert California: 'I thought you'd wear a sweater.' / Darryl: 'Since when does a sweater mean dressed up?' / Robert: 'Am I your grandson?'
jokes.setup: Robert defends his expectation that Darryl would wear a sweater
jokes.punchline: 'Am I your grandson?' — Robert deflects Darryl's objection by pointing out that only grandparents think sweaters are dressed-up, positioning himself as too sophisticated for that assumption
jokes.explanation: Robert's 'Am I your grandson?' is a compact, elegant retort — it reframes 'sweaters = dressed up' as a grandparent-level expectation with perfect economy. Highly quotable as a standalone line.

jokes.text: Robert California: 'Come on, stay, all right? It's good for people to get to know you. As a contestant on Dancing with the Stars, maybe.'
jokes.setup: Robert is trying to convince Darryl to stay at the upstairs party despite the tuxedo embarrassment
jokes.punchline: The encouragement ends with the qualifier that the tuxedo would only be appropriate if Darryl were a Dancing with the Stars contestant — a backhanded compliment that undercuts the whole pep talk
jokes.explanation: Good Robert California line — the 'Dancing with the Stars' qualifier is a very specific pop culture reference that works because it's an unexpected comparison and because Robert delivers it with his characteristic mixture of encouragement and condescension.

jokes.text: Oscar's grandmother at the upstairs party: 'I want my sugar-free cookie, and then I want a sugar cookie. And then I want my nap. That's right.'
jokes.setup: Oscar has brought his grandmother to the party
jokes.punchline: The grandmother's extremely specific and unapologetic cookie agenda — delivered as a series of non-negotiable demands ending in 'That's right' — is a small character revelation of comic perfection
jokes.explanation: A small gem — the specificity of wanting both a sugar-free AND a regular sugar cookie, followed by 'then I want my nap,' is a perfectly constructed micro-character moment. 'That's right' as self-affirmation is the button. This character appears for seconds and makes a strong impression.

jokes.text: Robert California: 'She is remarkable.' — referring to Oscar's grandmother after her cookie speech
jokes.setup: Oscar's grandmother finishes her cookie demand
jokes.punchline: Robert's sincere admiration ('She is remarkable') for an old lady making cookie demands at a party — his inability to distinguish between the genuinely impressive and the mundane is characteristic
jokes.explanation: Quick reaction beat — Robert's unironic admiration for the grandmother's assertiveness is a nice character-specific touch. Not a major joke but lands.

jokes.text: Erin to Darryl: 'How many drinks have you had tonight? I can't be driving everybody home.' — Darryl: 'A thousand.' / 'Whoa! Maybe you should take a break.' / 'Maybe you should mind your own business.' [pause] 'Just kidding.'
jokes.setup: Drunk Erin is trying to perform responsible party behavior while clearly intoxicated herself
jokes.punchline: Darryl's 'A thousand' is hyperbolic and deadpan; his 'Maybe you should mind your own business' is genuinely sharp before being defused by 'Just kidding' — the full reversal of roles (the drunk one policing the sober one) is the underlying joke
jokes.explanation: Good comedic reversal — the trashed Erin acting as designated responsible party is the ironic context, and Darryl's 'A thousand' is deadpan gold. The 'Just kidding' button adds a beat.

jokes.text: Dwight dramatically announces he's been attacked — 'someone put a porcupine in my drawer!' — then tells the full story of reaching for his 'toothbrush and some tooth powder'
jokes.setup: Dwight claims to be the victim of a porcupine-based prank
jokes.punchline: The combination of 'tooth powder' (not toothpaste — very Dwight) and the dramatic 'bloodthirsty rabid creature' framing of a porcupine is character-dense comedy
jokes.explanation: 'Tooth powder' is an excellent Dwight detail — the kind of character-specific historical affectation that makes the character funny without requiring a setup. His dramatic framing of the porcupine as 'bloodthirsty' and 'rabid' is also very Dwight.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I wonder, in this office, who has access to a porcupine? Or who in this office knows that I have access and is trying to set me up?'
jokes.setup: Dwight is publicly theorizing about who put the porcupine in his drawer
jokes.punchline: His second theory — that someone knows HE has access to a porcupine and is framing him — accidentally reveals that Dwight does in fact have access to a porcupine (which he later confirms by naming it)
jokes.explanation: This is smart comedy writing — Dwight's detective reasoning inadvertently confesses to owning a porcupine. The structure is: question about who has a porcupine → follow-up that implies Dwight does → full confirmation later when he names it Henrietta. The self-undermining logic is peak Dwight and requires attention to land fully.

jokes.text: Toby: 'You know, this sounds a lot like the premise of my latest Chad Flenderman novel, A Murder for Framing. Chad Flenderman. Just an easy-going black guy who knows the streets, yet he also went to Oxford. So just as comfortable on a motorcycle as he is on Air Force One.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is laying out the porcupine conspiracy
jokes.punchline: Toby derails the conversation to promote his novel and describe his mystery protagonist — the absurdly over-qualified Chad Flenderman, who combines every cool archetype simultaneously
jokes.explanation: The Chad Flenderman character description escalates perfectly — 'easy-going black guy who knows the streets, yet went to Oxford' alone is funny, but 'as comfortable on a motorcycle as he is on Air Force One' is the absurdist peak. Toby inserting his novel into a crisis is quintessential Toby. Rich character comedy.

jokes.text: Toby adds: 'Oh, and he's also the world's leading egyptologist.'
jokes.setup: Toby has just described Chad Flenderman as a street-smart Oxford man comfortable on Air Force One
jokes.punchline: One more credential: world's leading Egyptologist — a completely unrelated and maximally specific achievement tacked on as an afterthought
jokes.explanation: The 'world's leading Egyptologist' is the perfect final credential because it's simultaneously the most specific and the most useless relative to the other qualifications (street cred, Oxford degree, Air Force One comfort). Its complete non-sequitur nature and the matter-of-fact delivery make it the best escalation beat in the episode. Economy is nearly perfect — four words that recontextualize everything before them. This is textbook list comedy escalation.

jokes.text: Dwight to Toby: 'Nobody cares about your sex-crazed black detective.' / Toby: 'No, no, no, no, no, women chase him. He misses his wife.'
jokes.setup: Dwight dismisses Toby's novel description
jokes.punchline: Dwight characterizes Chad Flenderman as 'sex-crazed' (based on no evidence) — Toby's indignant correction ('women chase HIM' / 'he misses his wife') is a more dignified (and sadder) characterization that doesn't fully refute Dwight
jokes.explanation: Dwight's reductive dismissal is funny, but Toby's defensive clarification adds layers — 'he misses his wife' is a quietly sad detail that suggests Toby has poured his own loneliness into his fictional character. Works on the cringe/character level.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I wonder, in this office, who has access to a porcupine?' — then later is asked if the porcupine has been quilled — 'Yes, I was quilled.' / 'And what's its name?' / 'Henrietta.' / 'Oops.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is the apparent victim of a porcupine prank; Animal Control is called
jokes.punchline: The Animal Control officer asks for the porcupine's name — Dwight answers 'Henrietta' without hesitation, definitively confirming he owns the porcupine and staged the whole thing. 'Oops.' is Dwight's tiny acknowledgment of being caught.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best structured joke. The setup spans the entire porcupine sequence: Dwight claims to be the victim, nearly reveals he owns a porcupine via his second theory, then completely unmasks himself by knowing the porcupine's name when asked. 'Henrietta. Oops.' is a perfect two-word confession — 'Oops' is the entire acknowledgment of defeat, delivered deadpan. The structure (plant the reveal across multiple beats, let the character expose themselves) is masterful and deeply in character for Dwight. The 'Oops' is one of the episode's most quotable moments.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Fingerprints can be planted. You know, with a severed hand—' [everyone stares] 'Do you think that's what happened? Do you think he used a severed hand?'
jokes.setup: Andy says Jim's 'fingerprints are all over' the porcupine prank
jokes.punchline: Dwight takes 'fingerprints all over it' literally and proposes that Jim used a severed hand to plant them — then asks if others genuinely believe this
jokes.explanation: Dwight's literal-minded paranoia taken to a logical extreme — of course fingerprints could be planted with a severed hand. His genuine curiosity about whether others believe this is great. Classic Dwight absurdist logic.

jokes.text: Angela about the porcupine: 'You might want to run that by Angela. 'Cause it's so cute.' [Angela] 'No. Porcupines don't have souls. They're like dogs.'
jokes.setup: Someone suggests running the porcupine's fate by Angela since she loves animals
jokes.punchline: Angela — known for loving cats — has a very specific hierarchy: cats have souls, porcupines don't, and dogs are soulless too. Her casual 'they're like dogs' as a category of the soulless is perfect
jokes.explanation: Excellent Angela joke. 'They're like dogs' — delivered as though this settles the matter — is a perfect encapsulation of her cat supremacist worldview. The theological framework (souls) applied to animal taxonomy is very specific and funny. Could only be Angela.

jokes.text: Animal control asks the porcupine's name; Dwight answers 'Henrietta,' then says 'Oops.' Andy: 'What?' Dwight: [silence]
jokes.setup: Animal control asks if the porcupine has a name; Dwight claims the porcupine was a random attacker
jokes.punchline: 'Henrietta' slips out immediately, revealing that Dwight knows — and named — the porcupine, meaning HE planted it himself. 'Oops' is his only response.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect comedic structure. The reveal is achieved with a single word ('Henrietta'), followed by one word of response ('Oops'), followed by the camera/Andy processing it. The economy is extraordinary — the entire con is undone in one syllable. This is the kind of joke that rewards the viewer who was already suspicious of Dwight. The 'What?' that follows and Dwight's silence is the perfect button. Comparable in craft to the Dwight-planted-evidence jokes of the show's peak years.

jokes.text: Drunk Erin to Jim and Pam: 'I am so happy you guys are together. And you both have such beautiful hair. I hope you guys get married. And who knows? Maybe at the wedding I meet someone.'
jokes.setup: Erin approaches Jim and Pam, now clearly drunk
jokes.punchline: Erin's warm but slightly off-target compliments culminate in immediately redirecting to her own romantic prospects at their potential wedding — she's not at the wedding yet and they're already married
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny drunk Erin moment — the obliviousness of wishing Jim and Pam get married (they are married) and the pivot to hoping to meet someone at the wedding is character-specific. Not a strong joke structurally but lands as a character beat.

jokes.text: Erin: 'Okay, well, I'm gonna go do another reverse spit. That's how the cool kids say get a drink.'
jokes.setup: Erin is wrapping up her drunk interaction with Jim and Pam
jokes.punchline: 'Reverse spit' as slang for drinking — another Erin neologism, this one with slightly different logic (you spit things out, drinking is the reverse), delivered with pride
jokes.explanation: Another Erin coinage that works beautifully. 'Reverse spit' has actual internal logic (you spit liquid out; drinking is taking it in — the reverse). Her claiming this is 'how the cool kids say it' implies she has heard this from no one and invented it in the moment. The character integration is nearly perfect — this phrase is completely impossible from any other character.

jokes.text: Andy watching Erin be drunk: 'That's, uh, that's the girl you dated.' / Jim: 'Um, yeah, she's not really like that.' / Andy: 'She seems fun.' / Jim: '...Yeah, uh, excuse me.'
jokes.setup: Andy observes drunk Erin with Jim, his ex-girlfriend's ex
jokes.punchline: Jim's uncomfortable 'she's not really like that' (defending Erin's normal personality), Andy's cheerful 'She seems fun' (meaning the drunk version), and Jim's immediate exit — a small cringe exchange that implies Jim's lingering feelings
jokes.explanation: Subtle cringe beat — Jim's defensiveness about Erin's normal personality and his quick exit reads as mild discomfort. Works as a character moment more than a structured joke.

jokes.text: Drunk Erin to Andy: 'I don't want to put you out, but if someone's making oatmeal, I'll take an apple cinnamon and a maple brown sugar in one bowl with whole milk.'
jokes.setup: Andy offers to help drunk Erin, suggesting oatmeal
jokes.punchline: Erin's elaborate, specific oatmeal order — two flavors combined, with whole milk — delivered after the caveat 'I don't want to put you out' is an escalating absurdity
jokes.explanation: Good Erin drunk beat — the specific oatmeal order after 'I don't want to put you out' is a well-structured contradiction, and combining two specific flavors with whole milk is detailed enough to be funny.

jokes.text: Erin drunk at the bar: 'Every Martini has an olive.' [in response to 'have you had anything besides candy canes?']
jokes.setup: Someone asks drunk Erin if she's eaten anything besides candy canes
jokes.punchline: 'Every Martini has an olive' — treating the olive as a legitimate food group, a completely sincere defense of her diet
jokes.explanation: Very economical — five words that perfectly capture drunk Erin's logic. 'Every Martini has an olive' is one of the episode's more quotable lines. The sincerity of her nutritional reasoning is the joke.

jokes.text: Erin: 'I'd said I wish Jessica was dead.' / Andy: 'You — you mean you wish she wasn't here or something.' / Erin: 'I wish she was in a graveyard under the ground with worms coming out of her mouth.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks Erin what her Christmas wish is
jokes.punchline: Erin's death wish for Jessica escalates from the stark 'I wish Jessica was dead' to the viscerally specific 'under the ground with worms coming out of her mouth' — Andy tries to soften it, she doubles down with graphic detail
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is excellent: start with the blunt death wish, give Andy the chance to soften it ('you mean she wasn't here'), then Erin responds with cartoonishly specific grave imagery ('under the ground with worms coming out of her mouth'). The escalation from murder to worms is hilariously over-the-top, and it's deeply Erin — she's not calculating, just drunk and emotionally unfiltered. The grotesque specificity ('worms coming out of her mouth') is what elevates this from a simple dark joke to a memorable image. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Erin: 'You promised it would come true. You wrote it in an email! So which one are you, a murderer or a liar?'
jokes.setup: Andy tells Erin she can't wish for Jessica's death
jokes.punchline: Erin presents a binary: if Andy promised wishes come true, he must either commit murder or be a liar — the false dilemma delivered with drunk earnestness is perfectly Erin
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. 'Which one are you, a murderer or a liar?' is one of the most quotable lines in the episode, delivered with Erin's characteristic earnest logic. The false dilemma is internally consistent from Erin's perspective (she genuinely believes he promised to fulfill wishes), and 'you wrote it in an email!' grounds the absurdity in bureaucratic reality. The structure — accusation, evidence, binary ultimatum — is tight and lands hard.

jokes.text: Darryl to female partygoer: 'You know? Don't listen to what anyone is saying. You look like a... A princess.' [clearly reaching for the compliment, landing on 'princess' awkwardly]
jokes.setup: Darryl in his tuxedo is now mingling and dispensing compliments
jokes.punchline: The long pause before 'princess' — he's clearly struggling to find something flattering and lands on something vaguely condescending
jokes.explanation: Minor cringe beat — the pause before 'princess' suggests Darryl is winging it and the compliment doesn't quite land. Not a strong joke but qualifies as a comedic moment.

jokes.text: Jim shows the defaced picture of Cece (his daughter) to a group, performing outrage — then gradually admits maybe he defaced it himself, 'by accident'
jokes.setup: Jim shows a defaced picture of his daughter Cece, implying Dwight did it, rallying outrage
jokes.punchline: Jim progressively loses confidence in his own prank ('it's a little out of focus — probably an accident') before admitting 'maybe it was me who did it. By accident.' — an extraordinarily weak exit from his own scheme
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy — Jim's prank scheme involves defacing a picture of his own daughter, which he immediately starts second-guessing in real time. 'It's a little out of focus — probably an accident' and 'maybe it was me who did it. By accident.' are perfect anti-climax beats. The escalation-reversal structure (build outrage → immediately collapse it) and Jim's embarrassed 'Merry merry' exit are both well-executed. This shows Jim capable of a bad prank, which is a good character moment.

jokes.text: Andy Santa hat-check: 'You all right, Santa?' — Andy asks himself/Robert two-friends-sleeping-together rhetorical question
jokes.setup: Robert asks Andy if he's okay; Andy pivots to a philosophical question
jokes.punchline: Andy poses the question 'Do you think two friends who are NOT sleeping together can stay friends?' — reversing the rom-com trope ('can they stay friends after sex?') in a way that reveals his worry about Erin without saying it
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat — Andy's inverted version of the classic question ('can friends stay friends WITHOUT sleeping together') is a good subversion. Robert's uncertain 'Mm, I don't know' is an appropriately unsatisfying answer.

jokes.text: Kelly leans into Jessica and whispers something — then Andy looks over and: 'Jessica, did you just fart?'
jokes.setup: Kelly has clearly been whispering something to Jessica to embarrass her in front of Andy
jokes.punchline: Andy, apparently primed by what he's heard, publicly asks Jessica if she farted — which would be an incredibly embarrassing thing to ask your serious girlfriend in front of colleagues
jokes.explanation: Kelly's scheme to embarrass Jessica by getting Andy to publicly ask if she farted is a perfectly executed cringe moment. The setup (whisper to Andy → Andy publicly asks Jessica) is economical and the payoff ('did you just fart?') is the kind of mortifying moment that makes cringe comedy work. 'And that is how it's done' from Kelly is a nice button.

jokes.text: Kelly: 'And that is how it's done.'
jokes.setup: Kelly's scheme to embarrass Jessica has succeeded
jokes.punchline: Kelly's satisfied self-congratulation — delivered as if she's completed a masterwork — for a fart prank is perfectly disproportionate
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Kelly scheme. 'And that is how it's done' as a summary of a fart prank is very Kelly — her sense of herself as a master operator applied to something juvenile.

jokes.text: Kelly after the fart accusation, in confessional: 'And that is how it's done.'
jokes.setup: Kelly has just publicly accused Jessica of farting
jokes.punchline: Her smug tutorial tone — as though this is a technique to be admired and replicated — elevates a petty act to an art form in her mind
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum comedic return. 'And that is how it's done' after a fart accusation is Kelly at peak petty-confidence. The tutorial framing of a social attack is perfectly Kelly. Extremely high economy score — this could not be said in fewer words and shouldn't be.

jokes.text: Robert's bartending: 'Oh, never considered myself a mixologist. Oh, this is daunting. I need a mortar, pestle, muddler. Does anyone have any chocolate shavings?'
jokes.setup: Oscar is put in charge of the bar but defers; Robert steps in
jokes.punchline: Robert's immediate demand for artisanal bartending tools and chocolate shavings for what is presumably a simple open bar is maximally pretentious and funny
jokes.explanation: Robert California being an insufferable mixologist is a good character beat — the mortar and pestle for office party drinks is a perfect escalation of his pretension.

jokes.text: Robert to Darryl about love advice: 'I've been married thrice, and each has ended in an acrimonious divorce. I'm not sure I'm the best person to give love advice.'
jokes.setup: Darryl asks Robert for love advice about his heart being broken
jokes.punchline: Robert's magnificent self-assessment — three marriages, three acrimonious divorces, delivered matter-of-factly — as a reason he perhaps shouldn't give advice is both honest and absurd
jokes.explanation: Robert's love-advice disqualification is a great character moment — the understatement of 'I'm not sure I'm the best person' after THREE acrimonious divorces is very Robert. 'Thrice' (rather than 'three times') is a nice word-choice character touch.

jokes.text: Robert to Darryl: 'When you do your make-up... how long does it take usually? 'Cause...' [implying Darryl takes too long on his makeup as relationship advice]
jokes.setup: Robert pivots from admitting he can't give love advice to attempting some advice anyway
jokes.punchline: His advice is a passive-aggressive implication that Darryl spends too long on makeup — which is both non-sequitur and oddly specific. The unfinished sentence ('Cause...') leaves the audience and Darryl hanging
jokes.explanation: Odd Robert California moment — his pivot to commenting on Darryl's makeup routine as relationship advice is a characteristically strange non-sequitur. Works as a Robert character beat more than a crafted joke.

jokes.text: Toby, still talking about Chad Flenderman: 'Chad Flenderman's kryptonite—' / Robert California: 'Whoa, we got a real Clarence Thomas here.'
jokes.setup: Toby continues to push his novel character into the conversation
jokes.punchline: Robert shuts down Toby by comparing him to Clarence Thomas — a Supreme Court Justice known for rarely speaking — implying Toby should be as silent
jokes.explanation: Sharp reference — calling Toby a 'real Clarence Thomas' (known for being famously silent on the Supreme Court bench) as a way of telling him to shut up is specific and clever. Robert's dismissal of Toby is always a good dynamic.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Thank God Erin's getting a ride home with Robert, 'cause she is trashed. And who better to drive her home than Robert? I mean, what a standup guy... Separating from his wife, showing up at the Christmas party in a track suit and a blazer.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to reassure himself that Erin is safe with Robert
jokes.punchline: His evidence that Robert is a 'standup guy' — currently separating from his wife and wearing a track suit to the Christmas party — completely undermines his own reassurance
jokes.explanation: Good self-undermining character comedy — Andy building the case for Robert as trustworthy by citing evidence that does the exact opposite. The 'tracksuit and a blazer' detail is specific and visual. The structure (reassurance → evidence that undermines reassurance) is clean.

jokes.text: Meredith loading her junk/treasures into Andy's car as designated driver: 'It's my valuables! It's my treasures!' — Andy: 'You're a hoarder, my God!' — Meredith: 'No, I'm not! I'm gonna sell it on eBay!'
jokes.setup: Andy's bicycle designated driving plan has clearly failed; he's now driving Meredith home
jokes.punchline: Meredith has brought her 'treasures' to the office Christmas party and is insisting on loading them into Andy's car — the escalating argument about whether it's hoarding or eBay inventory
jokes.explanation: Functional Meredith character comedy — her insistence that her hoarded items are 'treasures' for eBay is a believable detail for her character. Physical comedy of loading junk into Andy's car works on screen.

jokes.text: Dwight to his porcupine in the parking lot: 'What are we gonna do with all that bonus money, Henrietta, huh?'
jokes.setup: Dwight is alone with his porcupine after the party
jokes.punchline: Dwight conspiratorially discusses bonus money with his porcupine — the bonus he doesn't have and presumably won't get — as if Henrietta is his partner in the scheme
jokes.explanation: Lovely coda to the Henrietta thread — Dwight treating his porcupine as a co-conspirator and already planning what to do with bonus money he hasn't won is pure Dwight. The character integration is exceptional. His optimism in the face of clear failure is endearing.

jokes.text: Meredith, in the car: 'Where are we? This ain't my street.' / Andy: 'Shh, shh, shh, shh.' / Meredith: 'Mmm, this is the posh part of town, huh?'
jokes.setup: Andy is driving Meredith home but has clearly taken a detour
jokes.punchline: Meredith recognizing she's not near her home but calmly noting it's 'the posh part of town' — her drunk acceptance of the situation and Andy's frantic shushing imply he's up to something
jokes.explanation: Minor scene beat — the suggestion that Andy is taking Meredith somewhere other than home (possibly checking on Erin/Robert) is amusing but not a fully formed joke.

jokes.text: Andy pulls up outside Robert California's house and sees Erin and Robert on the porch — 'Oh, my God.' [camera reaction implied]
jokes.setup: Andy has detoured to Robert's house to check on Erin
jokes.punchline: Whatever Andy sees on the porch provokes an 'Oh, my God' — the audience doesn't know what he sees but his reaction implies something suggestive is happening
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe setup — the audience is meant to assume something untoward is happening between Erin and Robert. The reaction shot is a visual gag that depends on what we don't see, which is classic mockumentary structure.

jokes.text: Andy driving away: 'Wonder what a studio condo would cost in this neighborhood.' / Meredith: 'Meredith, shut your drunk hole right now.'
jokes.setup: Andy has seen something distressing at Robert's house and is trying to process it
jokes.punchline: 'Shut your drunk hole' — a colorful Andy Bernard coinage for 'shut up,' delivered with uncharacteristic sharpness, immediately followed by Meredith's oblivious real estate speculation
jokes.explanation: 'Shut your drunk hole' is an excellent Andy coinage — specific, inventive, and uncharacteristically aggressive for him, which makes it funnier. Meredith's property valuation in the middle of an emotional crisis is a good counterpoint.

jokes.text: Robert dropping off Erin: giving her very specific instructions — 'Take a few aspirin, drink a whole lot of water, sleep in in the morning' — then when she thanks him and says good night, he stays in the car smiling suggestively
jokes.setup: Robert has driven drunk Erin home; he gives her detailed recovery instructions like a parent
jokes.punchline: His lingering smile after she goes inside suggests he's entertained — or perhaps more — by the situation; combined with the tracksuit detail, this is deeply ambiguous and uncomfortable
jokes.explanation: The cringe here is sustained and earned — Robert's paternal care instructions followed by a lingering, ambiguous smile is very uncomfortable comedy. The 'What are you smiling for?' and 'I'm sure I am not' exchange amplifies the discomfort perfectly.

jokes.text: Robert on Erin's porch: 'What are you smiling for? You thinking what I'm thinking?' / Erin (slightly fearful/excited): 'I'm sure I am not.' / Robert: 'Let's get you home.' / Erin: 'Ow! Take it easy!'
jokes.setup: Robert and Erin are saying goodnight; the audience (and Andy) suspects something may happen
jokes.punchline: Robert's leading question ('you thinking what I'm thinking?') is maximally sinister, Erin's response is fearful and resigned, and then Robert just... helps her home and she yelps 'Ow! Take it easy!' — suggesting he grabbed her arm to help her walk, not anything untoward, but the context makes it maximally uncomfortable
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe comedy — Robert's leading question is genuinely alarming, Erin's 'I'm sure I am not' is a perfect fearful response, and the 'Ow! Take it easy!' punchline recontextualizes everything as innocent while still feeling deeply uncomfortable. This is classic Office cringe: maximum discomfort, ambiguous but ultimately innocent payoff.

jokes.text: Dwight wakes up from a nap at his desk: 'Oh, man! Ah, fell asleep. Took a nap. Hey, guys. I feel refreshed now.' [to the empty office]
jokes.setup: The party has ended and most people have gone home
jokes.punchline: Dwight woke up at his desk from a party nap, announces he feels refreshed, and apparently has no idea what has happened — or what he missed
jokes.explanation: Dwight napping at his desk during the Christmas party and waking up refreshed while everyone else has left is a good character beat — deeply Dwight. Works as a closing joke for his arc.

jokes.text: Dwight helps himself to the leftover party cookies: 'Mmm, cookies. What's everyone staring at?'
jokes.setup: Dwight wanders the empty post-party office
jokes.punchline: 'What's everyone staring at?' when there's clearly no one there — Dwight is unaware of or unbothered by the empty room, addressing a non-existent audience
jokes.explanation: Good closing Dwight beat — 'What's everyone staring at?' addressed to an empty room is either obliviousness or Dwight performing normalcy for the camera. Both readings are funny. The economy of the line is excellent.

jokes.text: Jim talking head: 'Oh, man! I was supposed to tell Dwight something.' [long pause] 'Come on, Jim...' [another pause] 'I got nothing.'
jokes.setup: Jim was supposed to tell Dwight that Andy had lifted the bonus threat
jokes.punchline: Jim forgot to tell Dwight, which means Dwight spent the whole party behaving — and Jim didn't even have the excuse of a prank; he just forgot. Jim's self-directed 'Come on, Jim...' and 'I got nothing' are a perfect closing confessional
jokes.explanation: Strong closing joke. Jim's self-directed 'Come on, Jim...' as he tries and fails to excuse himself, followed by the defeated 'I got nothing,' is a perfect character note — he's embarrassed by his own oversight, not for pranking reasons, just incompetence. The pauses (inferred from the transcript) make this land. Good structural payoff to the A-plot.

tmdb_overview: Andy attempts to make everyone's Christmas wishes come true, including those of a drunken Erin. Meanwhile, Dwight and Jim are entangled in an escalating prank war wherein one attempts to frame the other.
